newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Libyan plane flies to Ghana despite U.N. ban.
newsitem.headline: Libyan plane flies to Ghana despite U.N. ban.

text.p: A Libyan plane flew an official delegation to Ghana's capital Accra on Tuesday in defiance of a 1992 United Nations ban on Libya's international flights, the official news agency JANA said on Wednesday.
JANA, monitored in Tunis, said the plane carried a foreign ministry delegation which was greeted in Accra by an adviser to President Jerry Rawlings and a Ghanaian foreign ministry official.
A Ghanaian government official confirmed the brief trip and said it took place on Tuesday.

Earlier on Wednesday, Libya said it had told the Security Council that it considered itself no longer subject to the air embargo after it gave permission for an American-piloted balloon to overfly its territoruy last week.

"The Libyan delegation was here briefly to hold consultations on the impending ministerial conference of the OAU (Organisation of African Unity)," Ghanian deputy foreign minister Mohamed Chambas told Reuters.
"They came in their own plane and we held a brief meeting and they went back. Tomorrow we are going to brief Security Council ambassadors (in Ghana) on the whole affair," he added.
OAU ministers are due to meet in Tripoli later this month.

Chambas did not identify the Libyan officials on the trip, but a Libyan delegation led by Foreign Minister Omar Mustafa al-Montasser who has been touring West Africa in recent days. JANA said he held talks in Namibia on Wednesday.

Ghana's President Rawlings who first seized power as a radical young air force officer has had close ties with Libya's revolutionary leader Muammar Gaddafi. Rawlings was re-elected last month for a second four-year term as civilian head of state.
An airport source witnessed the visit of the Libyans.
"A Libyan Boeing 727 arrived here at 8.39 p.m. (2039 GMT) yesterday and left at 11 p.m.," he said, adding that officials later removed records of the flight.

Libya has on several occasions violated a ban on international flights which is part of sanctions imposed by the United Nations in 1992 after it refused to hand over two Libyans indicted in the United States and Britain for their alleged role in the bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988 killing 270 people.

JANA said earlier on Wednesday: "(Libya) has informed the Security Council that the Arab Libyan airlines will continue its international flights and (Libya will) open its airspace to aircraft from other states after it permitted U.S. citizen Steve Fossett's balloon to cross the Libyan airspace."
It said a Libyan diplomat had handed a letter setting out Tripoli's position to the Security Council chairman and asked that it be circulated as an official document of the council.
A U.N. sanctions committee source on Tuesday rejected the Libyan claim, saying it was a "lot of hot air".

Libya first denied Fossett permission to overfly the country, but later changed its position. According to Fossett's control centre in Chicago, he was over Libya for an hour and 45 minutes though the detour and loss of fuel forced him to cut short his attempted around-the-world flight in India.
